Season a bland story with added flavour
Forgive a small and honest mistake

Harsh, unsparing and critical in review
Consumed with envy and bitter jealousy

Formally trained and licensed to practise medicine

Refuse ever to read the fine print
Fall asleep while on active duty

Surviving almost unchanged from remote antiquity
Gifted from early childhood with rare musical talent

Deeply silent and reserved by nature

Dismiss a loyal employee on the spot

Go back to lessons in an art class
Take a long and well-earned break

Savings kept carefully hidden at home
idioms.origin: The image of coins so 'hot' with temptation they burn through the fabric until spent.

To resign formally from one's post

options: Perfectly round and smooth in shape

words.note: Latin bellum = war (same root as 'belligerent' and 'rebellion').

Traced in a perfect, unbroken circle
Deeply moving and rich in emotion
words.usage: The plot was so convoluted that viewers needed a flowchart to track the twists.

options: A scarcity or lack of something
A deep, narrow valley between hills

options: To clear from blame; to justify
words.usage: The final results vindicated her decision to skip coaching and self-study.
words.note: Latin vindicare = to claim, avenge. To reclaim your good name.

idioms.idiom: Bite off more than you can chew
idioms.caption: Ambition: 10/10. Jaw capacity: 3/10.
options: Take on more than you can handle
Eat greedily and far too quickly

idioms.usage: Signing up for five test series at once? You've bitten off more than you can chew.

The very coldest, darkest point of the winter
The finest and choicest part of something good
A situation of extreme, delicate fragility

Parched and utterly dry, lacking all moisture
Legally binding and enforceable on all parties

options: A feeling of weariness and boredom
A swelling sense of pride and honour
A sudden, giddy rush of enthusiasm

options: To crush completely flat by force
To ornament to gaudy, showy excess

Let tired pets rest quietly indoors
Put off a decision for far too long

words.note: Greek boukolos = cowherd. Literally 'of cowherds'.

words.note: Latin culpa = fault, blame. As in 'mea culpa' — my fault.

options: To belittle or speak of dismissively
To split apart into separate parts
To fade gradually from public view
To contend in formal, staged debate
words.usage: Don't disparage 'easy' questions — they're the ones that decide percentiles.

Wounded deeply and left badly scarred
Unable to arrive at any firm decision

To pack tightly into a travel trunk
To brace or strengthen a structure
To address in a rude, curt manner
words.usage: The speaker truncated his talk when the fire alarm went off mid-slide.

A sudden family quarrel at home
idioms.origin: Traced to Cicero's Latin phrase about 'stirring up waves in a wine ladle' — outrage in a tiny vessel.

A closing summary of main points

Rare manuscripts from the ancient world

To read aloud before an audience

A senior judge chosen by popular election

To make a very hasty exit
words.usage: Toppers extol the power of revision; strugglers extol the power of new material.

Devoid of any real skill or talent

Touched with a quiet, gentle sorrow

words.usage: Her limpid prose made even tax law feel readable.
words.note: Latin limpidus = clear. Used for water, eyes, and enviably clear writing.

words.usage: The clause allowed dismissal for acts of moral turpitude.
words.note: Latin turpis = shameful. A favourite of legal documents everywhere.

idioms.idiom: Don't count your chickens before they hatch
idioms.caption: Eggs: 5. Chickens: pending.
options: Don't assume success before it happens
Never let good food go to waste needlessly
Plan the family finances early and well
Avoid rearing farmyard animals at home
idioms.origin: From Aesop's fable of the milkmaid who daydreamed of riches from unhatched eggs — and spilled the milk.
idioms.usage: He was choosing his IIM hostel room before results day — counting chickens before they hatch.

idioms.caption: Looks harmless. Isn't.
options: A dangerous person pretending to be harmless
A person dressed in poor, shabby clothing
A shy but quietly strong and firm leader
A police officer working deep undercover
idioms.origin: From Aesop and the Bible — a predator disguised in a sheep's fleece to sneak into the flock.
idioms.usage: The 'friendly' rival offering free notes with wrong answers — a wolf in sheep's clothing.

options: Able to reason at lightning speed
Legally answerable in a court of law
words.usage: Be cognizant of the sectional timer — many students lose marks to the clock, not the questions.
words.note: Latin cognoscere = to know. Awareness in its Sunday best.

options: Standing second in formal rank or order
Fragrant and sweet-smelling as spring blossom
Readily taken in and very easily fooled
words.usage: The 1920s were a fecund decade for physics — relativity, quantum theory, and more.
words.note: Latin fecundus = fruitful. Applies to soil, minds, and creative periods.

options: Gleaming and lustrous, like pure gold
Old, threadbare and long worn out
words.usage: The argument rested on gossamer evidence — one anonymous tweet.
words.note: From 'goose summer' — the season when spiders' silk threads drift through the air.

words.usage: A perspicacious reader spots the author's bias in the very first paragraph.
words.note: Latin perspicere = to see through. X-ray vision for ideas.

options: A bright shade of golden yellow
words.usage: After the monsoon, the campus turns verdant almost overnight.
words.note: Latin viridis = green. Same family as 'verdure'.

idioms.idiom: Every cloud has a silver lining
idioms.caption: Bad day. Good edges.
options: Every difficulty carries some hope or benefit
Hidden wealth lies scattered all around us
The weather can change utterly in an instant
Outward appearances are very often deceptive
idioms.origin: From Milton's 1634 poem Comus, describing a dark cloud turning its 'silver lining' to the moonlight.
idioms.usage: The low mock score stung, but the silver lining was a crystal-clear error list to work on.

idioms.caption: Less announcing. More doing.
options: What you do matters more than what you say
Shouting the loudest wins most arguments
Silence is always a sure sign of weakness
Promises must be made loudly and in public
idioms.origin: The sentiment is ancient, but the exact English phrasing was popularised in a 19th-century sermon.
idioms.usage: He never posted study streaks online — actions speak louder than words, and so did his rank.

options: A gradual rise to high office
words.usage: Her business acumen turned a tiny tuck shop into a three-city franchise before she turned 25.
words.note: Latin acuere = to sharpen — the same root as 'acute'. Business acumen is the classic collocation.

options: To warn or scold in a firm, mild way
To dismiss from a job or post
To flatter slyly with a hidden motive
words.usage: The invigilator admonished the two students for whispering — a warning, not yet a report.
words.note: Gentler than 'rebuke', sterner than 'remind'. An admonition corrects; it doesn't humiliate.

words.usage: State your revision plan clearly — most mentors are amenable to a schedule that shows real thought.
words.note: Collocation lock: amenable TO reason, TO change, TO suggestion. Positive valence — a cooperative openness.

words.usage: His answer in the interview was so anodyne that the panel forgot it before the door closed.
words.note: Greek an- (without) + odynē (pain). Literally a painkiller; figuratively, prose with the pain — and the point — removed.

words.usage: An ardent quizzer, she tracked every college fest from Ahmedabad to Indore.
words.note: Latin ardere = to burn. The same fire glows in 'ardour' and 'arson'.

idioms.caption: Hands where everyone can see them — nothing slipped under the table.
idioms.origin: From card games: hands kept above the table (the 'board') proved no cards were being swapped below it.
idioms.usage: The scholarship selection was completely above board — criteria published, scores displayed, queries answered.

idioms.caption: Armoured everywhere — except the one spot that matters.
idioms.origin: Thetis dipped baby Achilles in the Styx to make him invulnerable — holding him by the heel she left dry. Paris's arrow found exactly that spot.
idioms.usage: Parajumbles are her Achilles' heel — 99th percentile everywhere else, coin-toss accuracy there.

words.usage: Scoring your personal best in the first mock — an auspicious start to the season.
words.note: Roman augurs read bird-flight (avis = bird) for omens. A good reading made the day auspicious.

words.usage: Avarice, not need, drove him to bill clients for hours he never worked.
words.note: One of the seven deadly sins. Distinguish from 'miserliness': the miser hoards; the avaricious grasps for more.

words.usage: 'Hard work is the key to success' — a banal opener that essay checkers have read a thousand times.
words.note: Once meant 'common to all villagers' (the communal mill was 'banal'). Common → commonplace → stale.

options: Bored to the point of sleep
words.usage: He stared, bemused, at the DI set — the trap is reading 'bemused' as 'amused' in RC too.
words.note: Exam trap: bemused ≠ amused. It means confused. Verbal sections love testing this pair.

words.usage: After the topper left, the study group felt bereft of both direction and confidence.
words.note: Collocation: bereft OF hope, OF ideas. Nuance vs 'devoid': bereft lost what it once had; devoid never had it.

idioms.caption: One drop settles the question: real gold or fool's gold?
idioms.origin: Gold prospectors used nitric acid: real gold resists corrosion, fakes fizz and fail. The acid gave the final verdict.
idioms.usage: Mocks build you, but the three-hour actual paper is the acid test of your temperament.

idioms.caption: No compass, no coastline, no clue.
options: Away on a very long voyage
idioms.origin: From the age of sail: a ship out of sight of land, with no bearings, was 'all at sea' — position unknown, direction guessed.
idioms.usage: Without the formula sheet he was all at sea in the interest-rate questions.

words.usage: Copying the topper's answer sheet — with his name still on it — was brazen even by his standards.
words.note: Literally 'made of brass'. Brass doesn't blush; a brazen person can't either.

words.usage: His brusque 'Next question' cut off the doubt session — efficient, but it stung.
words.note: From Italian brusco = sour, sharp. Brusqueness is rudeness through shortness, not through insult.

options: A soft glow of warm light
words.usage: 'Your CR accuracy is the problem, not your speed' — mentors owe you that kind of candour.
words.note: Latin candor = whiteness, purity. The same root gives 'candid' and 'candle'.

options: To invest a large sum at once
To summarise briefly at the end
words.usage: After three hours of debate, the committee capitulated and moved the fest to February.
words.note: From Latin capitulum (chapter): surrender terms were drawn up under headings. 'Recapitulate' shares the root but not the defeat.

words.usage: Any 'mentor' who guarantees a 99th percentile for a fee is a charlatan — percentiles can't be promised.
words.note: From Italian ciarlare = to babble. The quack's patter came before his fake cures.

idioms.caption: Two heads, one collision course, zero compromise.
options: Working closely on a hard task
Bound by an old, bitter promise
idioms.origin: A 'loggerhead' was a long-handled iron ball heated for melting tar — and handy as a weapon when sailors brawled.
idioms.usage: The two section heads are at loggerheads over whether mocks should get harder or more frequent.

idioms.caption: The deadline is the twelfth stroke — and you arrive on the eleventh.
options: During the quiet of late night
idioms.origin: From the Biblical parable of the vineyard: labourers hired at the eleventh hour — one hour before day's end — were still paid in full.
idioms.usage: The application went in at the eleventh hour — submitted at 11:58 pm against a midnight deadline.

options: Calm in the face of danger
words.usage: A 95th percentile in one mock made him complacent; the next mock corrected that.
words.note: Trap pair: complacent (dangerously satisfied) vs complaisant (obligingly agreeable). One vowel, different exams of character.

options: To overlook or tacitly accept a wrong
To condemn loudly and in public
To reduce or cut short a legal sentence
words.usage: By staying silent about the leaked paper, the committee effectively condoned it.
words.note: Condoning isn't approving — it's letting a wrong pass unchallenged. RC authors lean on this nuance.

words.usage: A phone on the desk is not conducive to a three-hour deep-work block.
words.note: Collocation lock: conducive TO growth, TO learning, TO sleep. Positive valence — it helps things happen.

words.usage: Until the official key is out, every cut-off prediction is conjecture.
words.note: Latin conicere = to throw together. A conjecture is thrown together from hints, not built from proof.

options: Deeply sorry for a wrong done
words.usage: His contrite apology to the class — unprompted and specific — repaired most of the damage.
words.note: Latin conterere = to grind down. Genuine remorse grinds the ego; 'contrition' is its noun.

idioms.caption: The friendly favour hides a sharpening wheel.
options: A skill honed over many years
idioms.origin: From a tale by Benjamin Franklin: a stranger's flattery tricked a boy into sharpening the man's axe for free. Flattery, it turned out, had a motive.
idioms.usage: His 'neutral feedback' on the rival coaching app wasn't neutral — he had an axe to grind.

idioms.caption: The handshake ended years ago; the chill never did.
idioms.origin: Medieval medicine blamed emotions on bodily fluids: lasting hatred was thought to literally corrupt the blood.
idioms.usage: There's been bad blood between the two batches since the intercollege quiz controversy.

words.usage: Credulous aspirants forward every 'leaked paper' message; sceptical ones check the source.
words.note: Trap pair: credulous (believes too easily) vs credible (believable). The person is credulous; the story is credible.

words.usage: Her one-line reply — 'Check the second para again' — was cryptic, but it cracked the RC.
words.note: Greek kryptos = hidden, as in 'crypt' and 'cryptocurrency'. Hidden meaning, not just short length.

words.usage: A cursory read of the RC costs you the inference questions — skimming is a technique, not a shortcut.
words.note: Latin currere = to run (cursor, course). A cursory glance runs over the surface.

options: Casual to the point of rudeness
words.usage: He walked into the GD in a crisp blazer, debonair and unhurried, and owned the first minute.
words.note: Old French de bon aire = 'of good disposition'. Usually describes men; pairs well with 'suave'.

words.usage: What began as feedback became a ten-minute diatribe against 'this generation's attention span'.
words.note: A diatribe attacks; a tirade rants; a harangue lectures. All long, all loud — the diatribe is the most bitter.

idioms.caption: Brilliant plan. Now — who walks up to the cat?
options: To take on a risky task for the group
To warn everyone of fast-coming danger
To set a trap for an enemy
idioms.origin: Aesop's mice agree a bell on the cat would warn them all — until one asks who'll tie it on. Silence. Planning is easy; executing is the risk.
idioms.usage: Everyone wants the timetable changed, but who'll bell the cat and tell the director?

idioms.caption: Clear sky. Calm day. Then — lightning.
options: A stroke of rare good luck
idioms.origin: Lightning from a cloudless ('blue') sky is nature's least predictable strike — no warning, no clouds, no time to brace.
idioms.usage: Her decision to drop out and take a gap year came as a bolt from the blue.

options: Ruled by a pair of leaders
words.usage: The novel is charming until it turns didactic — every chapter ends with a moral lecture.
words.note: Greek didaskein = to teach. Neutral in 'didactic methods'; negative when the teaching turns to sermonising.

words.usage: Confiscating phones for a week over one late submission struck everyone as draconian.
words.note: Draco's 7th-century BCE Athenian code prescribed death for trivial crimes. His name became the adjective.

words.usage: Marking 'their' as 'there' once is a slip; five times in one essay is an egregious pattern.
words.note: Latin e grege = 'out of the flock' — once meant remarkably good. Irony flipped it; now only the bad stands out.

options: To draw out a response or fact
words.usage: A good GD moderator elicits views from the quiet participants, not just the loud ones.
words.note: Homophone trap: elicit (draw out) vs illicit (illegal). Verbal papers bank on the confusion.

options: To praise beyond what is due
words.usage: Asked to elucidate, she redrew the Venn diagram — and the whole class finally saw it.
words.note: Latin lux, lucis = light. To elucidate is to shed light; 'lucid' prose is already lit.

idioms.caption: One bone, two dogs, endless growling.
options: The central cause of a dispute
A weak point in an argument
idioms.origin: Two dogs, one bone: the oldest fight in the world. The bone itself became shorthand for whatever keeps the quarrel alive.
idioms.usage: Sectional time limits remain the bone of contention between students and the test team.

idioms.caption: The weapon goes underground; the friendship comes back up.
options: To end a quarrel and make peace
To hide the evidence of a wrong
To save a weapon for later use
idioms.origin: A Native American peace custom: when war ended, weapons were literally buried as proof the fighting was over.
idioms.usage: After two silent months, the study partners buried the hatchet over one plate of vada pav.

words.usage: Nothing engenders trust in a batch like a mentor who admits an error in the key.
words.note: Latin generare = to beget. Feelings and conditions are engendered — respect, hope, resentment.

options: To use vague words to dodge commitment
To divide into exactly equal shares
To speak with a trembling voice
words.usage: Asked if the syllabus was complete, he equivocated: 'Broadly, in a sense, mostly.'
words.note: Latin aequus (equal) + vocare (to call): giving equal voice to both meanings. Politicians' native tongue.

words.usage: Her erudite essay quoted Amartya Sen and the NEP in the same paragraph — and made both fit.
words.note: Latin e-rudis = 'out of rawness'. Education planes the roughness away; 'rude' keeps the same root.

options: To chew slowly and with care
words.usage: Serious aspirants eschew 'shortcut' vocab lists in the last week — cramming 500 words in 5 days fools no exam.
words.note: Related to 'shy' via Germanic roots — to eschew is to shy away on principle, not from fear.

words.usage: The farewell eulogy for the retiring professor ran twenty minutes and felt too short.
words.note: Greek eu (good) + logos (speech). Delivered at funerals but not limited to them; the opposite pole of a diatribe.

idioms.caption: Same colour, maybe. Same thing? Not even close.
options: Cheap goods passed off as costly
Two things that always go together
idioms.origin: White chalk and white cheese can look alike at a glance — and share nothing else. The English have used the pair since the 14th century.
idioms.usage: The twins are chalk and cheese: one lives in the library, the other in the gym.

idioms.caption: The rooster said, the bull swore, and somehow nobody believes it.
options: A children's tale with a moral
A rumour that proves to be true
idioms.origin: Likely from The Cock and The Bull — rival English coaching inns whose travellers' tales grew taller with every telling.
idioms.usage: He gave the invigilator a cock and bull story about a cousin's wedding and a stolen admit card.

words.usage: CCTV footage exonerated the student accused of switching answer sheets.
words.note: Latin ex + onus = to unburden (onus = load, as in 'the onus is on you'). Guilt lifted, load removed.

options: To send off on a voyage
words.usage: A polite mail to the coordinator expedited the scorecard correction by a full week.
words.note: Latin ex + pes, pedis = to free the feet (from shackles). Freed feet move fast; 'impede' chains them again.

options: Having many different faces or aspects
words.usage: 'Just mark C everywhere' — a facetious tip that one credulous junior actually followed.
words.note: Party trick: 'facetious' contains a, e, i, o, u — once each, in order. Humour in the wrong register is its meaning.

options: To openly defy a rule or norm
To display in a showy manner
words.usage: He flouted the centre's device policy and paid for it with a debarred attempt.
words.note: THE classic confusable: flout (defy) vs flaunt (show off). You flaunt wealth; you flout rules. Exams recycle this endlessly.

options: Set free completely from all worry
words.usage: The last week before results is fraught with rumours — mute the groups, trust the portal.
words.note: Collocation lock: fraught WITH danger, tension, peril. Valence is negative — if you see 'fraught', expect trouble after it.

idioms.caption: One river behind you — and no road back.
options: To pass a point of no return
To take a needless, showy risk
idioms.origin: In 49 BCE Caesar marched his legion across the Rubicon river — an act of war against Rome. 'The die is cast,' he said. There was no undoing it.
idioms.usage: Resigning to prepare full-time — she crossed the Rubicon, and the family knew it.

idioms.caption: The third false alarm is the one that costs the flock.
options: To warn of a genuine danger
To frighten someone as a joke
idioms.origin: Aesop's shepherd boy shouted 'Wolf!' for fun twice too often. When the real wolf came, the village had stopped listening.
idioms.usage: He'd cried wolf about 'guaranteed paper leaks' so often that no one checked his one real tip.

options: Excessive to the point of insincerity
Generous in a quiet, genuine way
Rich and satisfying, like a full meal
words.usage: His fulsome praise of the judges — 'visionaries, legends, giants' — embarrassed even the judges.
words.note: Trap: fulsome praise is NOT a compliment in careful usage — it's flattery so thick it curdles.

options: Relevant and fitting to the matter
Free from any infection or disease
words.usage: Keep GD points germane to the topic — one brilliant but irrelevant stat can sink your score.
words.note: Collocation lock: germane TO the argument, TO the issue. Originally 'having the same parents' — related, hence relevant.

options: Costing far more than it is worth
words.usage: The reviewer's gratuitous jab at the author's accent had nothing to do with the book.
words.note: From Latin gratis = free. A gratuitous insult is 'free' — unpaid-for, unprovoked, unnecessary.

words.usage: He cleared the group task by guile — quietly assigning himself the only role that gets noticed.
words.note: 'Guileless' — without guile — is the honest cousin. Beguile (to charm/deceive) grew from the same root.

words.usage: Her imperious wave silenced the back benches before the mock GD began.
words.note: Trap pair: imperious (domineering) vs imperial (of an empire) vs impervious (unaffected). Three lookalikes, three meanings.

idioms.caption: Nobody bet on it. It finished first anyway.
idioms.origin: From 19th-century racing: an unknown horse — kept 'in the dark' from bookmakers — could upset every calculation at the finish line.
idioms.usage: Quiet all year, she emerged as the dark horse of the batch with a 99.4 percentile.

idioms.caption: The fuse lit, the crowd leaned in... phhht.
idioms.origin: A squib is a small firework; wet, it fizzles instead of banging. Note the word — squib, not 'squid'. No sea creatures were disappointed.
idioms.usage: After a month of hype, the 'mega surprise test' was a damp squib — ten easy MCQs.

words.usage: Two crashes of the test portal, one power cut — the proctor stayed imperturbable throughout.
words.note: Im + perturb + able: cannot be perturbed. The interview panel's favourite quality to test with rapid-fire stress questions.

options: Unable to be affected or penetrated
Quick to take offence at slights
words.usage: Stay impervious to the toppers' WhatsApp flexes — their percentile isn't your syllabus.
words.note: Collocation lock: impervious TO criticism, TO water, TO logic. Im + per + via: no way through.

options: Just begun; not yet fully formed
words.usage: Her start-up plan is still inchoate — a name, a napkin sketch, and conviction.
words.note: Trap: inchoate ≠ chaotic, despite the look. It means embryonic — early, unformed, but not necessarily messy.

options: Harmful in a gradual, hidden way
Impossible to see with the eye
words.usage: Doomscrolling is insidious — no single reel hurts, and then the mock is tomorrow.
words.note: Latin insidiae = ambush. The insidious threat sits in wait; contrast 'invidious' (causing resentment).

words.usage: An intrepid few chose the unseen-poem section; fortune, this time, favoured them.
words.note: In (not) + trepidus (alarmed) — the exact opposite of 'trepidation', a word you already own.

idioms.caption: Today's menu: one large slice of 'I was wrong'.
options: To accept a very small share
To lose one's appetite from shame
idioms.origin: 'Umbles' were deer innards — servants' food while lords ate venison. Eating (h)umble pie meant being put in your place; the pun did the rest.
idioms.usage: After mocking the 'easy' paper he scored 60th percentile — and ate humble pie in the group chat.

idioms.caption: Right fish. Wrong element.
options: A person exposed as a fraud
A talent wasted on a small stage
Someone rescued right at the very last moment
idioms.origin: Chaucer used it in the 1380s: a monk away from his cloister was like a fish out of its element — gasping, graceless, wrong.
idioms.usage: A Gujarati-medium topper in an all-English GD, he felt like a fish out of water for exactly one week.

options: To dry out over a long period
words.usage: The helpline was inundated with calls the hour the results portal glitched.
words.note: Latin unda = wave (as in 'undulate'). Inboxes, helplines and towns get inundated alike.

options: Sweet to the point of excess
words.usage: The farewell video was pure lachrymose engineering — slow piano, old photos, zero dry eyes.
words.note: Latin lacrima = tear. Lachrymose films are 'tear-jerkers' in formal dress.

words.usage: The mendacious claim of a '100% selection rate' didn't survive one RTI query.
words.note: Latin mendax = lying. A mendacious person tells lies; a mendicant begs. Don't merge them.

options: To make less severe or serious
To argue a case in court
words.usage: You can't undo a weak Quant section, but a strong VA section mitigates the damage.
words.note: Trap: 'mitigate against' is an error — that's 'militate against'. Mitigate takes a direct object.

options: To shape by hand, as clay
words.usage: A same-day corrected scorecard mollified the furious parents faster than any apology.
words.note: Latin mollis = soft (as in 'emollient'). You mollify a person; you mitigate a problem.

idioms.caption: All spark, no shot.
options: A sudden burst of genuine talent
A quick meal made in a hurry
An idea stolen at the last minute
idioms.origin: In flintlock muskets, gunpowder in the 'pan' sometimes flashed without firing the shot — spectacle without result.
idioms.usage: One viral reel doesn't make a career; without consistency it's a flash in the pan.

idioms.caption: 'Any horse you like — as long as it's this one.'
options: The luxury of too many options
idioms.origin: Thomas Hobson, a Cambridge stable keeper, rented horses in strict rotation: take the one nearest the door, or take none.
idioms.usage: With every other slot full, the 8 am centre was a Hobson's choice — take it or skip the attempt.

words.usage: A munificent alumnus funded fee waivers for twenty first-generation aspirants.
words.note: Latin munus = gift. More lavish than 'generous'; distinguish from 'magnificent', which is about splendour, not giving.

words.usage: The interviewer's question — 'Sell me this silence' — left him utterly nonplussed.
words.note: Latin non plus = 'no more' (can be said). Trap: careless usage treats it as 'unfazed' — exams test the correct, opposite sense.

options: Quick to take up new ideas
words.usage: Obdurate on the retest question, the board didn't budge even after the error was proven.
words.note: Latin durus = hard (endure, durable). Harder than 'stubborn' — obduracy resists even moral pressure.

options: Stated as true, but perhaps not
words.usage: The ostensible reason was 'technical maintenance'; the actual reason leaked by evening.
words.note: Kin to 'ostentatious' (both from ostendere, to show) — but ostensible shows a surface story, not wealth.

words.usage: Her error log — dated, coded, reviewed weekly — is the paragon all mentors now cite.
words.note: Originally a touchstone for testing gold. A paragon is what everything else is tested against.

idioms.caption: No wind, no waves, no progress — just drift.
options: In a spell of gloom or stagnation
idioms.origin: The Doldrums are the windless equatorial belt where sailing ships stalled for weeks — going nowhere, slowly.
idioms.usage: Post-results, the whole batch was in the doldrums until the new season's first mock shook them awake.

idioms.caption: The scent is strong — and completely wrong.
options: An early warning sign of danger ahead
idioms.origin: Smoked herrings turn red and reek; dragged across a trail, one could pull hounds off the real scent — by design.
idioms.usage: In CR, that tempting statistic in option B is a red herring — it's true, but irrelevant to the conclusion.

words.usage: Parsimonious with marks, that examiner treats a 7/10 as an act of charity.
words.note: Beyond frugal: the frugal save wisely; the parsimonious hoard grudgingly. 'Parsimony' in science = economy of explanation.

options: Relating to lasting damage in bone
words.usage: The pernicious myth that 'toppers don't sleep' has ruined more attempts than any hard paper.
words.note: Latin pernicies = destruction. Pernicious harm works quietly and deep — pair it with 'insidious' in your notes.

words.usage: Only three people were privy to the surprise mock's date — somehow the whole batch knew.
words.note: Collocation lock: privy TO secrets, TO the plan. From 'private'; the Privy Council heard the monarch's private business.

words.usage: Twenty years of invigilation without one scandal — his probity is the department's quiet asset.
words.note: Latin probus = good, honest ('probe' and 'prove' are cousins). Probity is honesty that has been tested.

words.usage: Prodigal with his stipend in week one, he studied on borrowed data by week three.
words.note: Double trap: not 'prodigy' (genius), and the prodigal son is famous for wasting, not for returning.

idioms.caption: So clean it looks factory-new.
idioms.origin: From shipbuilding: a 'spick' (spike-nail) and 'span' (fresh wood chip) — a vessel of brand-new nails and timber, straight off the docks.
idioms.usage: Keep the error log spick and span — a messy log hides the very patterns it exists to reveal.

idioms.caption: One last song, saved for the very end.
options: A final performance before the end
A false, empty promise of retirement
A tune that brings good luck
idioms.origin: Ancient legend held that the mute swan sings once — beautifully — just before death. False zoology, immortal metaphor.
idioms.usage: The retiring professor's last lecture was his swan song — the hall was packed to the doors.

options: To write out in full detail
words.usage: The institute proscribed smartwatches after one too many 'fitness tracker' incidents.
words.note: THE prefix trap: proscribe = ban; prescribe = order/recommend. A doctor prescribes; a censor proscribes.

words.usage: Twenty minutes past the scheduled start, the restive hall began a slow clap.
words.note: Trap: restive does NOT mean restful — nearly its opposite. A restive crowd is one signature away from unrest.

words.usage: 'Bold strategy,' came the sardonic reply, 'attempting RC last with eight minutes left.'
words.note: Legend blames a Sardinian herb whose poison twisted faces into a grin. Darker and more contemptuous than 'sarcastic'.

words.usage: 'More attempts always means more marks' — specious logic that negative marking punishes.
words.note: Latin speciosus = fair-seeming. A specious argument is CR's favourite villain: plausible surface, hollow core.

words.usage: The unctuous salesman praised 'your visionary parenting' before quoting the course fee.
words.note: Latin unguere = to anoint (ointment, unguent). Literal oiliness became moral oiliness — flattery you can almost feel on the skin.

idioms.caption: Magnificent. Sacred. Ruinously expensive to feed.
options: A very rare stroke of fortune
A gift given with true love
idioms.origin: Siamese kings gifted sacred white elephants to courtiers they disliked: the animal couldn't work or be sold, yet cost a fortune to keep.
idioms.usage: The unused smart-board in every classroom became the campus's favourite white elephant joke.

idioms.caption: Everything everywhere, none of it in order.
options: In a state of tense waiting
idioms.origin: From a medieval dice game: betting on 'six and seven' (cinque and sice) was the most reckless wager — inviting chaos.
idioms.usage: New pattern, new portal, new timings — week one left even the teachers at sixes and sevens.
